arXiv:2606.19268v1 [math.ST] 17 Jun 2026

Patnaik-Pearson intrinsic dimension for internal representations of neural networks

Tom Hadfield Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Imperial College London Affiliation: 180 Queen’s Gate, London SW7 5HF, United Kingdom Email: t.hadfield@imperial.ac.uk
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We define a new measure of intrinsic dimension of a data manifold, which we call the Patnaik-Pearson dimension, and apply this to internal representations of neural networks, in particular transformers. The inspiration for this comes from the HTSR and SETOL work of Martin, Mahoney and Hinrichs, combined with the TwoNN intrinsic dimension estimator of Facco et al. We prove various properties of this intrinsic dimension estimator. Treating weight matrices of neural networks as data manifolds, for weight matrices whose Empirical Spectral Density follows a Pareto (Power Law) distribution, we relate the Patnaik-Pearson dimension to the HTSR and SETOL analysis, and show that critical values of the tail exponent coincide for the two approaches. Using a combination of theoretical and numerical techniques, we study the behaviour of the Patnaik-Pearson dimension of a data manifold under the transformations typical to neural networks. We apply this machinery to the BERT-base and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1 models, to investigate first the Patnaik-Pearson dimension of the initial data manifold of token embeddings, and second the evolution of the Patnaik-Pearson dimension as token embeddings pass through the layers of the model. Code and notebooks used for the numerical results presented here is available at https://github.com/tdhadfield/PatnaikPearson

1 Introduction

In this paper we develop machinery for studying the evolution of the data manifold of internal representations of a neural network as it passes through the layers of the network, with particular application to the transformer architecture.

Mathematical understanding of neural networks, in particular transformers [33], is an area of intensive ongoing study by a number of mathematicians, with a variety of different approaches. In the work of Rigollet and coworkers [16, 32], the transformer is modelled as a mean-field interacting particle system on a spherical surface. The key mathematical tool here is the Wasserstein gradient flow. Tokens are particles, and each encoder layer is a discrete time-step of a continuity equation driven by a self-attention kernel. The long-time attractor is a point mass (corresponding to rank collapse and token uniformity), but there is a long-lived metastable phase of partial clustering. This relates to the measure-theoretic approach of Vuckovic et al [34], who interpret self-attention as a system of self-interacting particles.

Neural networks have been extensively studied from the viewpoint of Riemannian geometry. In [24] Menon describes the training dynamics for Deep Linear Networks in terms of the geometric theory of dynamical systems, unifying results by several authors into a thermodynamic framework for deep learning. In [7] Di Sipio, Diaz-Rodriguez and Serrano present a geometric framework for understanding transformer-based models, via an explicit analogy to General Relativity.

There are very active approaches via algebraic geometry. In [15] Kubjas, Li and Wiesmann study the geometry of polynomial neural networks with monomial activation functions. In [17] Grosdos and coworkers study rational neural networks using algebraic-geometric tools. When the activation function is polynomial, the corresponding function space, the “neuromanifold”, can be naturally described by polynomial equations and inequalities, enabling it to be studied algebraically. In [20] Marchetti et al. build the foundations of neuroalgebraic geometry, a research direction combining algebraic geometry and deep learning. They study neural networks with polynomial activations, for which the associated function spaces are semi-algebraic varieties, and outline the correspondence between algebro-geometric invariants of these varieties and fundamental aspects of machine learning.

Topological data analysis and persistent homology provide very valuable insights. For example, in [12], Fitz et al. study the evolution of internal topological structure in various LLMs across depth and time during training, finding surprising distinctions between the behaviour of transformer-based as compared to LSTM-based architectures. In [14], Gardinazzi and coworkers use zigzag persistence to build topological descriptors which measure how topological features develop, persist and evolve through the layers of the network. In [19] Magai and Ayzenberg study internal representations of neural networks and the dynamics of changes in the topology and geometry of the data manifold on different layers. We also mention the work of Fay et al [10] applying persistent homology to study how adversarial inputs to LLMs reshape the topology and geometry of their internal representation spaces.

Finally, we mention the neural operator approach of Boullé and Townsend [2]. Operator learning aims to discover or approximate an unknown operator, which often corresponds to the solution operator associated with an unknown PDE. Neural operators generalize neural networks by taking the inputs and outputs to be functions rather than vectors.

For a very clear and comprehensive description of the mathematics underlying the transformer architecture, we recommend the paper of Noguer I Alonso [25].

In this paper we take a different approach. A major motivation for the work presented here is the pioneering work of Martin, Mahoney and Hinrichs [22, 23] on Heavy-Tailed Self-Regularization (HTSR) and their Semi-Empirical Theory of Learning (SETOL). They first of all observed empirically [21] a recurring pattern of heavy-tailed distributions of eigenvalues in the weight matrices of well-trained models, and then developed a theoretical model for this phenomenom, using techniques from statistical physics, quantum chemistry and random matrix theory.

Taking this as a starting point, we are interested in measuring the intrinsic dimension of a data manifold, and how this evolves as it is acted upon by weight matrices with specific empirical spectral densities. The notion of intrinsic dimension of a data manifold is not uniquely defined. Recall that the Manifold Hypothesis [11, 35] is the hypothesis that high dimensional data tend to lie in the vicinity of a low-dimensional submanifold - this has been observed empirically in many real world situations, giving rise to the development of a wide range of statistical methods, and has been suggested as a key explanatory factor for the success of modern neural network architectures. Intrinsic dimension is the dimension of this submanifold, namely the true number of degrees of freedom of the data. In the context of internal data representation of neural networks, intrinsic dimension is the number of coordinates necessary to describe the data without meaningful information loss. It is well-known that deep neural networks are substantially over-parametrized, with significant redundancy among both weights and activations.

There are many different approaches to defining intrinsic dimension, using a wide range of mathematical tools and capturing different aspects of the data manifold. A very important example for this paper is the TwoNN intrinsic dimension estimator [9] of Facco et al. We also mention the L2N2 estimator of Ong et al. [26], which is proven to be universal, in the sense that it converges to the true intrinsic dimension independent of which distribution is used to generate the data. Finally, we mention the work of Ansuini et al. [1], on intrinsic dimension of data-representations internal to neural networks, who observe that for trained networks, intrinsic dimension first increases and then progressively decreases as the data representation passes through the layers of the network.

In this work we start by studying a simple Gaussian point cloud generative model for a data manifold XX, realised as a collection of NN points {𝐱1,𝐱2,…,𝐱N}\{\bfxone,\bfxtwo,...,\bfxN\} in ℝd\RR^{d}. Our original motivation for this model came from considering the question, what is the intrinsic dimension of the data manifold represented by the token embeddings of the BERT model [6]. We apply the TwoNN intrinsic dimension estimator [9] to this generative model, and show that another measure of dimension naturally emerges, which we call the Patnaik-Pearson intrinsic dimension of XX, due to its use of Patnaik and Pearson’s moment-matching formulae [18, 27, 28], and denote by PP(X)\PatnaikPearson(X). We study the properties of PP(X)\PatnaikPearson(X) for various behaviours of our generative model. Treating weight matrices of neural networks as data manifolds, for weight matrices whose Empirical Spectral Density follows a Pareto (Power Law) distribution, we relate the Patnaik-Pearson dimension to the HTSR and SETOL analysis. In particular, the critical values for the tail exponent for both the Patnaik-Pearson dimension and HTSR and SETOL coincide. Using a combination of theoretical and numerical techniques, we study the behaviour of the Patnaik-Pearson dimension of a data manifold under the transformations typical to neural networks - multiplication by weight matrices; application of activation functions and softmax; addition, interpolation and concatenation; layer normalisation; attention. A consistent phenomenom throughout is the fact that heavier-tailed distributions dominate lighter-tailed. Some of these operations typically decrease Patnaik-Pearson dimension, others tend to increase it. It remains an open question as to in what generality these results hold. The strongest observation here is our product hypothesis, Conjecture 4.1; namely that for AA and BB matrices in general position, with shapes N×dN\times d and d×nd\times n, and NN, dd, mm sufficiently large, then

1dPP(A)∗1mPP(B)≤1mPP(AB)≤min{1dPP(A),1mPP(B)}{\tfrac{1}{d}}\PatnaikPearson(A)*{\tfrac{1}{m}}\PatnaikPearson(B)\leq{\tfrac{1}{m}}\PatnaikPearson(AB)\leq\min\{{\tfrac{1}{d}}\PatnaikPearson(A),{\tfrac{1}{m}}\PatnaikPearson(B)\}

Finally, we apply this machinery to two examples - the BERT-base and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1 models, to study the Patnaik-Pearson dimension of the data manifold of token embeddings, and the evolution of the Patnaik-Pearson dimension as data passes through the layers of the model. Consistent with the observation of many previous studies, we observe that dimension decreases.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Random Matrices

We summarise some basic material about random matrices [29] that we use in the sequel.

Singular value decomposition: An N×dN\times d (real-valued) matrix AA can be decomposed as

A=U​S​VTA=USV^{T} (1)

where UU is an orthogonal N×NN\times N matrix, VV is d×dd\times d orthogonal and SS is a diagonal N×dN\times d matrix, with diagonal entries Si​i=λiS_{ii}=\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}, for 1≤i≤min⁡(N,d)1\leq i\leq\min(N,d), where the λi\lambda_{i} are the non-zero eigenvalues of A​ATAA^{T} (which coincide with the non-zero eigenvalues of AT​AA^{T}A).

Marchenko-Pastur distribution: Suppose WW is an d×nd\times n random matrix, whose entries are iid N⁡(0,σ2)N(0,\sigma^{2}), with σ2<∞\sigma^{2}<\infty. Define Y=1d​WT​WY={\tfrac{1}{d}}W^{T}W which is a symmetric n×nn\times n matrix, with non-negative eigenvalues λ1,…,λn\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n}. Then in the limit as n,d→∞n,d\rto\infty, keeping the aspect ratio c:=n/dc:=n/d constant, the probability distribution of the eigenvalues of YY converges to a Marchenko-Pastur distribution M​P​(c,σ2)MP(c,\sigma^{2}). This is supported on [λ−,λ+][\lambda_{-},\lambda_{+}], with

λ±=σ2​(1±c)2\lambda_{\pm}=\sigma^{2}(1\pm\sqrt{c})^{2} (2)

plus, if c>1c>1, an atom at 0 of mass 1−1c1-{\tfrac{1}{c}}. The pdf f⁡(x)f(x) is given by

f⁡(x)=(λ+−x)​(x−λ−)2​π​σ2​c​x,λ−≤x≤λ+f(x)=\frac{\sqrt{(\lambda_{+}-x)(x-\lambda_{-})}}{2\pi\sigma^{2}cx},\quad\lambda_{-}\leq x\leq\lambda_{+} (3)

and f⁡(x)=0f(x)=0 otherwise, apart from the possible atom at 0.

Pareto distribution: A real-valued random variable XX follows a Pareto (Power Law) distribution, with tail exponent α>0\alpha>0, if ℙ(X>x)=x−α\PP(X>x)=x^{-\alpha}, for x≥1x\geq 1. The corresponding pdf is

f⁡(t)=αtα+1,t≥1,f⁡(t)=0,t<1f(t)={\frac{\alpha}{t^{\alpha+1}}},\,t\geq 1,\quad f(t)=0,\,t<1 (4)

Subexponential distributions [3]: Suppose XX is a non-negative random variable, with CDF F⁡(x)=ℙ(X≤x)F(x)=\PP(X\leq x), and define F¯​(x)=1−F⁡(x)=ℙ(X≥x)\overline{F}(x)=1-F(x)=\PP(X\geq x). The distribution FF is subexponential if

F⋆F¯(x)∼2F¯(x)asx→∞\overline{F\star F}(x)\sim 2\overline{F}(x)\quad\mathrm{as}\quad x\rto\infty

This is equivalent to; if X1X_{1}, X2X_{2} are iid copies of XX, then

ℙ(X1+X2>x)∼2ℙ(X>x)\PP(X_{1}+X_{2}>x)\sim 2\PP(X>x)

And, further, FF is subexponential iff

ℙ(X1+X2>x)∼ℙ(max{X1,X2}>x)asx→∞\PP(X_{1}+X_{2}>x)\sim\PP(\max\{X_{1},X_{2}\}>x)\quad\mathrm{as}\quad x\rto\infty

Since X1,X2≥0X_{1},X_{2}\geq 0, max⁡{X1,X2}>x\max\{X_{1},X_{2}\}>x implies that X1+X2>xX_{1}+X_{2}>x, so subexponentiality is equivalent to

P(X1+X2>x∩max{X1,X2}≤x)=o(P(X1>x))asx→∞P(X_{1}+X_{2}>x\cap\max\{X_{1},X_{2}\}\leq x)=o(P(X_{1}>x))\quad\mathrm{as}\quad x\rto\infty

which is the “single big jump” principle for sums of subexponentially distributed random variables.

Furthermore, if the distribution FF is subexponential, then the pdf ff of XX is heavy-tailed, in the sense that

lim supx→∞f(x)eλ​x=+∞∀λ>0\limsup_{x\rto\infty}f(x)e^{\lambda x}=+\infty\quad\forall\quad\lambda>0

The Pareto distribution, as well as many other well-known distributions (e.g. Cauchy, Weibull, lognormal) are subexponential.

We need the following results, from [3, 4, 8]:

Theorem 2.1

Suppose X1X_{1} and X2X_{2} are heavy-tailed (subexponential) positive random variables, with tail exponents α1\alpha_{1} and α2\alpha_{2} respectively. Then:

  1. 1.

    The sum X1+X2X_{1}+X_{2} is subexponential, with tail exponent given by min⁡{α1,α2}\min\{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\}.

  2. 2.

    Provided α1≠α2\alpha_{1}\neq\alpha_{2}, then the product X1​X2X_{1}X_{2} is subexponential, again with tail exponent given by min⁡{α1,α2}\min\{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\}.

2.2 HTSR and SETOL

We give a brief summary of the Heavy-Tailed Self-Regularization (HTSR) and Semi-Empirical Theory of Learning (SETOL) work of Martin, Mahoney and Hinrichs [21, 22, 23].

We are concerned with the weight matrices at each layer of some Neural Network. Given a real-valued d×nd\times n weight matrix WW define YY to be the n×nn\times n correlation matrix

Y=1d​WT​WY={\frac{1}{d}}{W^{T}}W

The Empirical Spectral Density (ESD) of WW, denoted ρemp⁡(λ)\rhoemp(\lambda) is formed from the eigenvalues λj\lambda_{j} of YY:

ρemp⁡(λ)=1n​∑j=1nδ⁡(λ−λj)\rhoemp(\lambda)={\frac{1}{n}}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\delta(\lambda-\lambda_{j})

For randomly initialized weights, we would expect a Marchenko-Pastur distribution (2, 3). However, numerical results consistently show that, for the best-performing pre-trained models, the weight matrices (of all layers) have heavy-tailed ESDs, and that the tails of these ESDs can be fit well by a Pareto (Power Law) distribution, for some tail exponent α\alpha, beyond some cutoff λ0\lambda_{0}:

ρtail⁡(λ)=ρemp⁡(λ)∼λ−α,λ≥λ0\rhotail(\lambda)=\rhoemp(\lambda)\sim\lambda^{-\alpha},\quad\lambda\geq\lambda_{0} (5)

Note that this is a slightly different convention than used in (4), to avoid any confusion later in this paper note that the correspondence between the two is given by

αHTSR=αPareto+1{\alpha_{\HTSR}}={\alpha_{\Pareto}}+1 (6)

See also Section 4.1.

The HTSR theory states that a Neural Network layer is optimally trained when its ESD can be fit to a Power Law distribution, with tail exponent (in the sense of (5)) of α=2\alpha=2. Crucially, this appears to be a universal property of all well-trained Neural Networks, irrespective of training data, model architecture, and training procedure. Furthermore, empirical results show that α<2\alpha<2 (the so-called HTSR Very Heavy-Tailed class) characterises overfitting. In addition HTSR uses Random Matrix Theory to identify qualitatively-distinct phases of learning, classifying the ESD of a weight matrix WW into one of 5+1 Phases of Training, as follows:

  1. 1.

    Random: corresponds to the start of training - the randomly initialized weights given rise to a Marchenko-Pastur distribution for the ESD.

  2. 2.

    Bulk plus Spikes: as training progresses, larger eigenvalues (spikes) appear and separate themselves from the Marchenko-Pastur bulk.

  3. 3.

    Weakly Heavy-Tailed: a power-law distribution for the largest eigenvalues has developed, with tail exponent α>6\alpha>6.

  4. 4.

    Heavy (Fat) Tailed: as training continues, α\alpha steadily decreases, and now lies in the range 2<α<62<\alpha<6.

  5. 5.

    Very Heavy Tailed: 1<α<21<\alpha<2. This indicates overfitting.

  6. 6.

    Rank Collapse.

As discussed in [25, 31], the evolution of the ESD during training relates to the “grokking” phenomenom [30], where the initial phase of model training corresponds to memorization, and is characterised by high intrinsic dimension of weight matrices, followed by a sharp reduction in intrinsic dimension at the grokking transition. The very useful WeightWatcher package [21] computes various HTSR Layer Quality metrics. It is not fully understood why training via Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) produces heavy tails.

2.3 The TwoNN intrinsic dimension formula

We summarise the formulae given by Facco et al. [9]. For a detailed derivation, see Appendix 8.

Suppose we have a collection XX of NN points {𝐱1,…,𝐱N}\{\xsubone,\ldots,\xsubN\} in ℝd\RR^{d}, that lie on an mm-dimensional submanifold of ℝd\RR^{d}. We want to estimate mm. For a given point 𝐱i\xsubi, consider the list of its nearest neighbors. Let ri,1≤ri,2≤…r_{i,1}\leq r_{i,2}\leq\ldots be a sorted list of their distances from 𝐱i\xsubi. Thus ri,1r_{i,1} is the distance from 𝐱i\xsubi to its nearest neighbour, ri,2r_{i,2} is the distance to the second-nearest neighbour, and so on. For each ii, define μi=ri,2/ri,1\mu_{i}=r_{i,2}/r_{i,1}, the ratio of the distances from 𝐱i\xsubi to its second and first nearest neighbours. We think of {μi}1≤i≤N\{\mu_{i}\}_{1\leq i\leq N} as representing draws from the distribution of a random variable μ\mu. Then it can be shown (see [9], or the Appendix (8)), that the pdf and CDF of μ\mu are given by

f⁡(t)=m​t−(m+1)​𝟏[1,∞),F⁡(x)=(1−x−m)​𝟏[1,∞)f(t)=mt^{-(m+1)}{\bf{1}}_{[1,\infty)},\quad F(x)=(1-x^{-m}){\bf{1}}_{[1,\infty)} (7)
Definition 2.1

The Two Nearest Neighbors (TwoNN) estimator for the intrinsic dimension of XX is

TwoNN(X)=−𝔼(log⁡(1−F⁡(μ))log⁡(μ))=−1N∑i=1Nlog⁡(1−F⁡(μi))log⁡(μi)\TwoNN(X)=-\EE\left({\frac{\log(1-F(\mu))}{\log(\mu)}}\right)=-{\frac{1}{N}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}{\frac{\log(1-F(\mu_{i}))}{\log(\mu_{i})}} (8)

The algorithm for estimating this is as follows.

  1. 1.

    Compute the pairwise distances for all pairs of points in XX.

  2. 2.

    For each point 𝐱i\xsubi, find the two shortest distances ri,1r_{i,1} and ri,2r_{i,2}, and compute μi=ri,2ri,1\mu_{i}={\frac{r_{i,2}}{r_{i,1}}}.

  3. 3.

    Empirically estimate the cumulative distribution F⁡(x)F(x) by sorting the values μi\mu_{i} in ascending order.

  4. 4.

    Plot the points (log⁡(μi),−log⁡(1−F⁡(μi)))(\log(\mu_{i}),-\log(1-F(\mu_{i}))) in the plane, and fit a straight line passing through the origin. The estimate for TwoNN(X)\TwoNN(X) is the gradient of this line.

In the case where we have a single observation μ\mu, then we can estimate (8) as

TwoNN(X)=−log⁡(0.5)log⁡(μ)=log⁡(2)log⁡(μ)\TwoNN(X)=-{\frac{\log(0.5)}{\log(\mu)}}={\frac{\log(2)}{\log(\mu)}} (9)

3 The Patnaik-Pearson intrinsic dimension

We present a simple generative model for a data manifold, and define a new estimator for intrinsic dimension specifically for this situation, which we call the Patnaik-Pearson intrinsic dimension, denoted PP(X)\PatnaikPearson(X). This arises naturally from applying the TwoNN estimator to this model and then using Patnaik and Pearson’s moment-matching formulae. In practice we have found numerically, for synthetic data of known intrinsic dimension, that the TwoNN estimator underestimates the real intrinsic dimension (this seems to be well-known). We prove various properties of PP(X)\PatnaikPearson(X), in particular its behaviour when the ESD of XX follows a Pareto distribution.

3.1 A simple Gaussian point cloud generative model for a data manifold

Consider a simple generative model for our data manifold XX, realised as the collection X={𝐱1,…,𝐱N}X=\{\xsubone,\ldots,\xsubN\} of NN points in ℝd\RR^{d} defined as follows. Let 𝐱i=(xi,k)1≤k≤d\xsubi=(x_{i,k})_{1\leq k\leq d}, where xi,k∼λk​Zi,kx_{i,k}\sim\lambda_{k}Z_{i,k}, where the Zi,kZ_{i,k} are iid N⁡(0,1)N(0,1), and the scalars λ1\lambda_{1}, .. ,λd\lambda_{d} satisfy

0≤λ1≤λ2≤…≤λd0\leq\lambda_{1}\leq\lambda_{2}\leq\ldots\leq\lambda_{d}

Denote 𝝀=(λk)1≤k≤d\blambda=(\lambda_{k})_{1\leq k\leq d}. Obviously, this Gaussian point cloud model is a strong assumption about the shape of our data manifold and there are many data manifolds that do not correspond to this, but it is a useful model for our analysis.

The general question is, given some estimator ID(X)\ID(X) for the intrinsic dimension of XX, how does this depend on 𝝀\blambda? More precisely, can we find functions g1g_{1}, g2g_{2} that are lower and upper bounds (for sufficiently large NN and dd):

g1​(𝝀)≤ID(X)≤g2​(𝝀)g_{1}(\blambda)\leq\ID(X)\leq g_{2}(\blambda) (10)

In particular, for the situation where the λk\lambda_{k} are drawn from a Pareto distribution with tail density exponent α\alpha (4), we would like to characterise ID(X)\ID(X) in terms of α\alpha, i.e. find functions h1h_{1}, h2h_{2} such that

h1​(α)≤ID(X)≤h2​(α)h_{1}(\alpha)\leq\ID(X)\leq h_{2}(\alpha) (11)

We expect any sensible estimator ID(X)\ID(X) to have the following properties:

  1. 1.

    1≤ID(X)≤d1\leq\ID(X)\leq d, provided 𝝀≠𝟎\blambda\neq{\bf 0}.

  2. 2.

    For any mm with 0≤m≤d−10\leq m\leq d-1, if λ1=…=λd−m=0≠λd−m+1\lambda_{1}=\ldots=\lambda_{d-m}=0\neq\lambda_{d-m+1}, then ID(X)≤m\ID(X)\leq m.

  3. 3.

    For any mm with 0≤m≤d−10\leq m\leq d-1, if λ1=…=λd−m=0\lambda_{1}=\ldots=\lambda_{d-m}=0, and λd−m+1=…=λd≠0\lambda_{d-m+1}=\ldots=\lambda_{d}\neq 0, then ID(X)=m\ID(X)=m.

  4. 4.

    If we scale each λk\lambda_{k} by a strictly positive scalar ϕ\phi, then ID(X)\ID(X) will be unchanged.

  5. 5.

    ID(X)\ID(X) is invariant under rotations and translations of XX.

3.2 The generalised Chi-Squared distribution

We now apply the TwoNN estimator to our generative model and find that the Patnaik-Pearson estimator naturally emerges from our analysis. To find nearest neighbours we need to calculate the distances between points. The (squared) distance between two randomly chosen points 𝐱i\xsubi, 𝐱j∈X\xsubj\in X is given by

dist(𝐱i,𝐱j)2=‖𝐱i−𝐱j‖2=∑k=1dλk2​(Zi,k−Zj,k)2{\dist(\xsubi,\xsubj)}^{2}={||\xsubi-\xsubj||}^{2}=\sum_{k=1}^{d}\lambda_{k}^{2}(Z_{i,k}-Z_{j,k})^{2}

Now, Zi,k−Zj,k=2​Zi,j,kZ_{i,k}-Z_{j,k}=\sqrt{2}Z_{i,j,k}, for some Zi,j,k∼N⁡(0,1)Z_{i,j,k}\sim N(0,1). Hence

dist(𝐱i,𝐱j)2=2​∑k=1dλk2​Zi,j,k2{\dist(\xsubi,\xsubj)}^{2}=2\sum_{k=1}^{d}\lambda_{k}^{2}Z_{i,j,k}^{2} (12)

which is “Chi-squared with 2​(∑k=1dλk2)2(\sum_{k=1}^{d}\lambda_{k}^{2}) degrees of freedom”. For each point 𝐱i\xsubi we want to find the distances to its first and second neighbours, namely

ri,1=minj≠i⁡{dist(𝐱i,𝐱j)},ri,2=secondminj≠i{dist(𝐱i,𝐱j)}r_{i,1}=\min_{j\neq i}{\{\dist(\xsubi,\xsubj)\}},\quad r_{i,2}=\secondmin_{j\neq i}{\{\dist(\xsubi,\xsubj)\}}

Patnaik-Pearson moment-matching: Suppose that Zi∼N⁡(0,1)Z_{i}\sim N(0,1) are iid, for 1≤i≤d1\leq i\leq d. As before, assume that 0≤λ1≤λ2≤…≤λd0\leq\lambda_{1}\leq\lambda_{2}\leq\ldots\leq\lambda_{d}, and define the weighted sum of squares

Y=λ1​Z12+λ2​Z22+…+λd​Zd2Y=\lambda_{1}Z_{1}^{2}+\lambda_{2}Z_{2}^{2}+\ldots+\lambda_{d}Z_{d}^{2} (13)

This follows a Generalised Chi-Squared distribution. Patnaik [27] showed that this could be approximated (matching the first two moments of the distribution) by a scaled χ2\chi^{2}-distribution

Y∼c⋅χ2​(ν)∼Γ⁡(ν2,2​c)whereν=ν⁡(𝝀)=(∑i=1dλi)2∑i=1dλi2,c=c⁡(𝝀)=∑i=1dλi2∑i=1dλiY\sim c\cdot\chi^{2}(\nu)\sim\Gamma({\tfrac{\nu}{2}}, 2c)\quad\mathrm{where}\quad\nu=\nu({\blambda})={\frac{(\sum_{i=1}^{d}{\lambda_{i}})^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{i}^{2}}},\quad c=c({\blambda})={\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{d}{\lambda_{i}^{2}}}{\sum_{i=1}^{d}{\lambda_{i}}}} (14)

This was extended by (Egon) Pearson [28] to match the first three moments of the distribution. It is immediate that 1≤ν⁡(𝝀)≤d1\leq\nu(\blambda)\leq d, with the upper and lower bounds being realised by the cases λ1=…=λd≠0\lambda_{1}=\ldots=\lambda_{d}\neq 0; and λi=0\lambda_{i}=0 for all i≠di\neq d, respectively.

Now, Γ⁡(ν2,2​c)\Gamma({\tfrac{\nu}{2}}, 2c) has pdf given by

f(t)=1Γ⁡(ν2)2ν/2xν/2−1e−x/2,t>0f(t)={\frac{1}{\Gamma({\tfrac{\nu}{2}})}}2^{\nu/2}x^{\nu/2-1}e^{-x/2},\quad t>0 (15)

and hence, for xx small, CDF given by

F⁡(x)≈1Γ⁡(ν2+1)​(x2)ν/2F(x)\approx{\frac{1}{\Gamma({\tfrac{\nu}{2}}+1)}}{\left({\frac{x}{2}}\right)}^{\nu/2} (16)

Starting with Y∼c⋅χ2​(ν)Y\sim c\cdot\chi^{2}(\nu) , then χ2​(ν)\chi^{2}(\nu) has pdf proportional to tν/2−1e−t/2t^{\nu/2-1}e^{-t/2} so near t=0t=0,

CDFχ2​(ν)(t)∼1Γ⁡(ν2+1)​(t2)ν/2{\CDF}_{\chi^{2}(\nu)}(t)\sim{\frac{1}{\Gamma({\frac{\nu}{2}}+1)}}\left({\frac{t}{2}}\right)^{\nu/2}

So to solve CDFχ2​(ν)(x)=y\CDF_{\chi^{2}(\nu)}(x)=y, then

(x2)ν/2=y​Γ​(ν2+1)⟹x=2​y2/ν​(Γ⁡(ν2+1))2/ν\left({\frac{x}{2}}\right)^{\nu/2}=y\Gamma({\tfrac{\nu}{2}}+1)\quad\implies x=2y^{2/\nu}(\Gamma({\tfrac{\nu}{2}}+1))^{2/\nu}

Suppose we have a non-negative random variable XX. If we draw NN times from this distribution, obtaining X1X_{1}, X2X_{2}, .. , XNX_{N}, and define the first and second order statistics

X(1)=min⁡(X1,X2,…,XN),X(2)=secondmin(X1,X2,…,XN)X_{(1)}=\min(X_{1},X_{2},\ldots,X_{N}),\quad X_{(2)}=\secondmin(X_{1},X_{2},\ldots,X_{N})

Then

𝔼(X(1))=CDF−1(1N),𝔼(X(2))=CDF−1(2N)\EE(X_{(1)})={\CDF}^{-1}({\tfrac{1}{N}}),\quad\EE(X_{(2)})={\CDF}^{-1}({\tfrac{2}{N}})

Hence, for Y∼c⋅χ2​(ν)Y\sim c\cdot\chi^{2}(\nu), then ℙ(Y≤x)=ℙ(χ2​(ν)≤xc)\PP(Y\leq x)=\PP(\chi^{2}(\nu)\leq{\tfrac{x}{c}}), and CDFY(x)=CDFχ2​(ν)(xc){\CDF}_{Y}(x)={\CDF}_{\chi^{2}(\nu)}({\frac{x}{c}}). It follows that

CDFY−1(1N)=c​CDFχ2​(ν)−1(1N){\CDF}_{Y}^{-1}({\tfrac{1}{N}})=c\,{\CDF}_{\chi^{2}(\nu)}^{-1}({\tfrac{1}{N}})

Therefore

CDFY−1(2N)=c​CDFχ2​(ν)−1(2N)≈c​ 22/ν​CDFχ2​(ν)−1(1N)=22/ν​CDFY−1(1N){\CDF}_{Y}^{-1}({\tfrac{2}{N}})=c\,{\CDF}_{\chi^{2}(\nu)}^{-1}({\tfrac{2}{N}})\approx c\,2^{2/\nu}\,{\CDF}_{\chi^{2}(\nu)}^{-1}({\tfrac{1}{N}})=2^{2/\nu}\,{\CDF}_{Y}^{-1}({\tfrac{1}{N}})

hence

CDFY−1(2N)/CDFY−1(1N)≈22/ν{\CDF}_{Y}^{-1}({\tfrac{2}{N}})/{\CDF}_{Y}^{-1}({\tfrac{1}{N}})\approx 2^{2/\nu}

and thus, using (12),

μ=μ⁡(N):=CDFY−1(2N)/CDFY−1(1N)≈21/ν\mu=\mu(N):=\sqrt{{\CDF}_{Y}^{-1}({\tfrac{2}{N}})/{\CDF}_{Y}^{-1}({\tfrac{1}{N}})}\approx 2^{1/\nu}

Combining this with (9) gives

TwoNN(X)≈log⁡(2)log⁡(μ⁡(N))=log⁡(2)log⁡(21/ν)=ν⁡(𝝀)\TwoNN(X)\approx{\tfrac{\log(2)}{\log(\mu(N))}}={\tfrac{\log(2)}{\log(2^{1/\nu})}}=\nu(\blambda) (17)

This suggests that ν⁡(𝝀)\nu(\blambda) may be a useful proxy for TwoNN(X)\TwoNN(X).

3.3 The Patnaik-Pearson intrinsic dimension of a data manifold

Following (14, 17), we define a function ν:ℝ≥0d\{𝟎}→ℝ>0\nu:\RR_{\geq 0}^{d}\backslash\{{\bf 0}\}\rto\RR_{>0}, and use this to define the Patnaik-Pearson intrinsic dimension PP(X)\PatnaikPearson(X) of a (realisation of a) data manifold XX.

Definition 3.1

For 𝛌∈ℝ≥0d\{𝟎}\blambda\in\RR_{\geq 0}^{d}\backslash\{{\bf 0}\}, 𝛌=(λi)1≤i≤d\blambda={(\lambda_{i})}_{1\leq i\leq d}, define

ν⁡(𝝀)=(∑i=1dλi)2∑i=1dλi2\nu(\blambda)={\frac{(\sum_{i=1}^{d}{\lambda_{i}})^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{i}^{2}}} (18)

Obviously ν\nu extends to a function ℝd\{𝟎}→ℝ\RR^{d}\backslash\{{\bf 0}\}\rto\RR, but we want to emphasise the fact that we are assuming that all the λi\lambda_{i} are non-negative.

Lemma 3.1

The following properties of ν⁡(𝛌)\nu(\blambda) are immediate:

  1. 1.

    1≤ν⁡(𝝀)≤d1\leq\nu(\blambda)\leq d, with the upper and lower bounds being realised by the cases 0≠λ1=…=λd0\neq\lambda_{1}=\ldots=\lambda_{d}; and λi=0\lambda_{i}=0 for all i≠di\neq d, respectively.

  2. 2.

    For any mm with 0≤m≤d−10\leq m\leq d-1, if λ1=…=λd−m=0≠λd−m+1\lambda_{1}=\ldots=\lambda_{d-m}=0\neq\lambda_{d-m+1}, then ν⁡(𝝀)≤m\nu(\blambda)\leq m, with equality iff λd−m+1=…=λd≠0\lambda_{d-m+1}=\ldots=\lambda_{d}\neq 0.

  3. 3.

    For any ϕ>0\phi>0, then ν(ϕ𝝀)=ν(𝝀)\nu(\phi\blambda)=\nu(\blambda).

Definition 3.2

The Patnaik-Pearson intrinsic dimension PP(X)\PatnaikPearson(X) of a data manifold XX. Suppose we have a realisation of XX as NN points 𝐱1,𝐱2,…,𝐱N∈ℝd\bfxone,\bfxtwo,\ldots,\bfxN\in\RR^{d}, considered as an N×dN\times d matrix whose rows are the 𝐱iT\bfxi^{T}. Define 𝐱¯=𝟏𝐍​∑𝐢=𝟏𝐍𝐱i\xoverline={\tfrac{1}{N}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\bfxi, and define Xresid=X−𝟏N​𝐱¯𝐓\Xresid=X-{\bf 1}_{N}\xoverline^{T}, i.e. we subtract 𝐱¯\xoverline(as a row vector) from each individual row of XX. Then, using (1) we have Xresid=USVT\Xresid=USV^{T} where SS is a non-negative diagonal N×dN\times d matrix, with diagonal elements λi\lambda_{i}, for 1≤i≤d1\leq i\leq d, and UU and VV are real-valued orthogonal matrices, of dimension N×NN\times N and d×dd\times d respectively. We define the Patnaik-Pearson intrinsic dimension of XX as

PP(X)=ν⁡(𝝀)=(∑i=1dλi)2∑i=1dλi2\PatnaikPearson(X)=\nu(\blambda)={\frac{(\sum_{i=1}^{d}{\lambda_{i}})^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{i}^{2}}} (19)

Note that this resembles, but is distinct from, the stable rank of a matrix, which for Xresid\Xresid is

sr(Xresid)=‖Xresid‖F2/‖Xresid‖op2=∑i=1dλi2/λmax\stablerank(\Xresid)={\normXresid}_{F}^{2}/{\normXresid}_{op}^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{i}^{2}/{\lambda_{\max}} (20)

where λmax=max1≤i≤d⁡{λi}{\lambda_{\max}}={\max_{1\leq i\leq d}}\{\lambda_{i}\}.

Note also that we have defined PP(X)\PatnaikPearson(X) for an N×dN\times d data manifold XX, but the definition makes sense for any matrix, so given (dimensionally compatible) matrices AA, BB we can consider PP(A)\PatnaikPearson(A), PP(B)\PatnaikPearson(B) and PP(AB)\PatnaikPearson(AB). In particular we can apply this to the weight matrices WW of neural networks, and compare PP(XW)\PatnaikPearson(XW) with PP(X)\PatnaikPearson(X) and PP(W)\PatnaikPearson(W).

Definition 3.3

In the sequel we will also work extensively with the normalised Patnaik-Pearson dimension 1dPP(X){\tfrac{1}{d}}\PatnaikPearson(X), which we will sometimes refer to as “nu/d”.

Theorem 3.1

Provided X=XresidX=\Xresid, if OO is an orthogonal N×NN\times N matrix, and QQ an orthogonal d×dd\times d matrix, then

PP(OX)=PP(X)=PP(XQ)=PP(OXQ)\PatnaikPearson(OX)=\PatnaikPearson(X)=\PatnaikPearson(XQ)=\PatnaikPearson(OXQ) (21)

and further

PP(XT)=PP(X)\PatnaikPearson(X^{T})=\PatnaikPearson(X) (22)

Proof: These are all immediate from the definition. ■\myqed

We can generalise ν\nu to an extended version that we will use in the sequel:

Definition 3.4

For 𝛌∈ℝ≥0d\blambda\in\RR_{\geq 0}^{d}, λ=(λi)1≤i≤d{\bf{\lambda}}={(\lambda_{i})}_{1\leq i\leq d}, and s>0s>0, define

νs:ℝ≥0d→ℝ≥0,ν(𝝀)=(∑i=1dλis)2∑i=1dλi2​s\nu_{s}:{\RR}_{\geq 0}^{d}\rto{\RR}_{\geq 0},\quad\nu(\blambda)={\frac{(\sum_{i=1}^{d}{\lambda_{i}^{s}})^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{i}^{2s}}} (23)
Theorem 3.2

For fixed 𝛌\blambda, d​νs​(𝛌)d​s≤0{\frac{d\nu_{s}(\blambda)}{ds}}\leq 0, with equality iff λi=λj\lambda_{i}=\lambda_{j} for all ii, jj.

Proof: From the definition,

d​νs​(𝝀)d​s=2​(∑i=1dλis)(∑i=1dλi2​s)2​[(∑i=1dln⁡(λi)​λis)​(∑i=1dλi2​s)−(∑i=1dln⁡(λi)​λi2​s)​(∑i=1dλis)]{\frac{d\nu_{s}(\blambda)}{ds}}={\frac{2(\sum_{i=1}^{d}{\lambda_{i}^{s}})}{(\sum_{i=1}^{d}{\lambda_{i}^{2s}})^{2}}}\left[(\sum_{i=1}^{d}\ln(\lambda_{i})\lambda_{i}^{s})(\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{i}^{2s})-(\sum_{i=1}^{d}\ln(\lambda_{i})\lambda_{i}^{2s})(\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{i}^{s})\right] (24)

For ϕ>0\phi>0, νs(ϕ𝝀)=νs(𝝀)\nu_{s}(\phi\blambda)=\nu_{s}(\blambda). Without loss of generality assume that 0<λi≤10<\lambda_{i}\leq 1 for all ii. Hence λis≤1\lambda_{i}^{s}\leq 1, so λi2​s≤λis\lambda_{i}^{2s}\leq\lambda_{i}^{s} for all ii, therefore ∑i=1dλi2​s≤∑i=1dλis\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{i}^{2s}\leq\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{i}^{s}, with equality iff λi=1\lambda_{i}=1 for all ii. Thus (24) becomes

d​νs​(𝝀)d​s≤2​(∑i=1dλis)(∑i=1dλi2​s)2​[(∑i=1dln⁡(λi)​λis)​(∑i=1dλis)−(∑i=1dln⁡(λi)​λi2​s)​(∑i=1dλis)]{\frac{d\nu_{s}(\blambda)}{ds}}\leq{\frac{2(\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{i}^{s})}{(\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{i}^{2s})^{2}}}\left[(\sum_{i=1}^{d}\ln(\lambda_{i})\lambda_{i}^{s})(\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{i}^{s})-(\sum_{i=1}^{d}\ln(\lambda_{i})\lambda_{i}^{2s})(\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{i}^{s})\right]
=2​(∑i=1dλis)2(∑i=1dλi2​s)2​[∑i=1dln⁡(λi)​(λis−λi2​s)]={\frac{2(\sum_{i=1}^{d}{\lambda_{i}^{s}})^{2}}{(\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{i}^{2s})^{2}}}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{d}\ln(\lambda_{i})(\lambda_{i}^{s}-\lambda_{i}^{2s})\right]

and all terms are positive, apart from ln⁡(λi)≤0\ln(\lambda_{i})\leq 0, hence the product is ≤0\leq 0. Hence d​νs​(𝝀)d​s≤0{\frac{d\nu_{s}(\blambda)}{ds}}\leq 0. ■\myqed

We establish a further useful result:

Theorem 3.3

Suppose YY is a non-negative random variable with finite moments ek=𝔼(Yk)<∞e_{k}=\EE(Y^{k})<\infty for k=1,2k=1,2, and 𝔼(Y2)≠0\EE(Y^{2})\neq 0. Given iid Yi∼YY_{i}\sim Y, for i=1,2,…​di=1,2,\ldots d, define

h⁡(Y,d)=1d​(∑i=1dYi)2∑i=1dYi2=(1d​∑i=1dYi)21d​∑i=1dYi2h(Y,d)={\frac{1}{d}}{\frac{(\sum_{i=1}^{d}Y_{i})^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{d}Y_{i}^{2}}}={\frac{({\tfrac{1}{d}}\sum_{i=1}^{d}Y_{i})^{2}}{{\tfrac{1}{d}}\sum_{i=1}^{d}Y_{i}^{2}}}

limd→∞h(Y,d)=𝔼(Y)2𝔼(Y2)\lim_{d\rto\infty}h(Y,d)={\frac{\EE(Y)^{2}}{\EE(Y^{2})}} (25)

1d​∑i=1dYi→a.s𝔼(Y),1d​∑i=1dYi2→a.s𝔼(Y2){\tfrac{1}{d}}\sum_{i=1}^{d}Y_{i}\quad\rto^{a.s}\quad\EE(Y),\quad{\tfrac{1}{d}}\sum_{i=1}^{d}Y_{i}^{2}\quad\rto^{a.s}\quad\EE(Y^{2})

and (25) follows. To estimate the rate of convergence, for large dd,

1d​∑i=1dYi∼e1+σ⁡(Y)d​Z1⟹1d2​(∑i=1dYi)2∼e12+2​e1​σ​(Y)d​Z1+O⁡(1d){\tfrac{1}{d}}\sum_{i=1}^{d}Y_{i}\sim e_{1}+{\tfrac{\sigma(Y)}{\sqrt{d}}}Z_{1}\quad\implies\quad{\tfrac{1}{d^{2}}}(\sum_{i=1}^{d}Y_{i})^{2}\sim e_{1}^{2}+{\tfrac{2e_{1}\sigma(Y)}{\sqrt{d}}}Z_{1}+O({\tfrac{1}{d}})

and also, provided e3e_{3} and e4e_{4} are finite,

where Z1Z_{1}, Z2Z_{2} are N⁡(0,1)N(0,1). It follows that

=e12e2⁡[1+1d(2​σ​(Y)e1⁡Z1−σ⁡(Y2)e2⁡Z2)+O⁡(1d)]=\formulaFive (26)

=1d​σ​(Y)​σ​(Y2)Cov(∑i=1dYi,∑j=1dYj2)=1d(e3−e2​e1σ⁡(Y)​σ​(Y2))=1dCorr(Y2,Y)={\frac{1}{d\sigma(Y)\sigma(Y^{2})}}\Cov(\sum_{i=1}^{d}Y_{i},\sum_{j=1}^{d}Y_{j}^{2})={\frac{1}{d}}\left({\frac{e_{3}-e_{2}e_{1}}{\sigma(Y)\sigma(Y^{2})}}\right)={\frac{1}{d}}\Corr(Y^{2},Y)

with

3.4 Uniform distribution

Suppose the λi\lambda_{i} are drawn from a uniform U⁡[0,1]U[0,1] distribution. For Y∼U⁡[0,1]Y\sim U[0,1], then 𝔼(Yk)=1k+1\EE(Y^{k})={\tfrac{1}{k+1}}. Hence by (27),

h(Y,d)≈34[1+σ⁡(Q)dZ]asd→∞h(Y,d)\approx{\frac{3}{4}}\left[1+{\frac{\sigma(Q)}{\sqrt{d}}}Z\right]\quad{\mathrm{as}}\quad d\rto\infty (29)

with σ⁡(Q)=215\sigma(Q)=\sqrt{{\tfrac{2}{15}}}. So for large dd, 1d​ν​(𝝀)≈34{\frac{1}{d}}\nu(\blambda)\approx{\frac{3}{4}}, with standard deviation

3​σ​(Q)4​d=34​d​215=1d⋅32​10=0.2739d{\frac{3\sigma(Q)}{4\sqrt{d}}}={\frac{3}{4\sqrt{d}}}\sqrt{{\frac{2}{15}}}={\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}}\cdot{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{10}}}={\frac{0.2739}{\sqrt{d}}}

This is confirmed numerically by Figure 3 (b) - here the predicted and observed standard deviations are 0.0274 and 0.0272 respectively.

3.5 Marchenko-Pastur distribution

For Y∼MP(c,σ2)Y\sim\MP(c,\sigma^{2}), then 𝔼(Y)=σ2\EE(Y)=\sigma^{2}, and Var(Y)=σ4​c\Var(Y)=\sigma^{4}c, hence 𝔼(Y2)=σ4​(c+1)\EE(Y^{2})=\sigma^{4}(c+1) Hence if we draw our λi\lambda_{i} from the distribution of YY, then applying (27) we have

ν(𝝀)≈d​(σ2)2σ4​(c+1)=dc+1⟹limd→∞1dν(𝝀)=1c+1\nu(\blambda)\approx{\frac{d(\sigma^{2})^{2}}{\sigma^{4}(c+1)}}={\frac{d}{c+1}}\quad\implies\quad\lim_{d\rto\infty}{\frac{1}{d}}\nu(\blambda)={\frac{1}{c+1}} (30)

Figure 4 gives numerical confirmation of this, for a range of values of cc and dd.

3.6 Pareto distribution with tail exponent α\alpha

Suppose the λi\lambda_{i} are drawn from a Pareto distribution with tail exponent α>0\alpha>0 (4), i.e. ℙ(λ>x)=x−α\PP(\lambda>x)=x^{-\alpha}, for x≥1x\geq 1. The corresponding pdf is

f⁡(t)=αtα+1,t≥1,f⁡(t)=0,t<1f(t)={\frac{\alpha}{t^{\alpha+1}}},\,t\geq 1,\quad f(t)=0,\,t<1 (31)

Define

s=1α,C⁡(α)=(1−2​s)(1−s)2=α⁡(α−2)(α−1)2,α≠1s={\frac{1}{\alpha}},\quad C(\alpha)={\frac{(1-2s)}{(1-s)^{2}}}={\frac{\alpha(\alpha-2)}{(\alpha-1)^{2}}},\,\,\alpha\neq 1 (32)
Theorem 3.4

Define ν∞(α)=limd→∞1dν(α,d)\nuinfty(\alpha)=\lim_{d\rto\infty}{\tfrac{1}{d}}\nu(\alpha,d). Then

ν∞(α)={C⁡(α):α≥20:α≤2\nuinfty(\alpha)=\left\{\begin{aligned} C(\alpha)\,:\,\alpha\geq 2\\ 0\,:\,\alpha\leq 2\end{aligned}\right. (33)

This is illustrated in Figure 5.

Proof: For α>2\alpha>2, by Theorem 3.3, ν∞​(α)\nu_{\infty}(\alpha) = 𝔼(λ)2/𝔼(λ2)\EE(\lambda)^{2}/\EE(\lambda^{2}), with

𝔼(λ)=αα−1,𝔼(λ2)=αα−2\EE(\lambda)={\frac{\alpha}{\alpha-1}},\quad\EE(\lambda^{2})={\frac{\alpha}{\alpha-2}}

and the result follows.

For 2>α>12>\alpha>1, then 𝔼(Y)\EE(Y) is finite, but 𝔼(Y2)\EE(Y^{2}) is infinite. By Kolmogorov’s SLLN [8],

1d∑i=1dλi→a.s𝔼(λ)<∞,1d∑i=1dλi2→a.s∞{\tfrac{1}{d}}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{i}\rto^{a.s}\EE(\lambda)<\infty,\quad{\tfrac{1}{d}}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{i}^{2}\rto^{a.s}\infty

Hence 1dν(α,d)→0{\tfrac{1}{d}}\nu(\alpha,d)\rto 0 as d→∞d\rto\infty.

For 1>α1>\alpha, then both 1d​∑i=1dλi{\tfrac{1}{d}}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{i} and 1d​∑i=1dλi2{\tfrac{1}{d}}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{i}^{2} diverge, however in this extremely heavy tailed situation, the largest value λmax\lambda_{\max} dominates both terms [4], with ν⁡(α,d)≈(λmax)2λmax2=1\nu(\alpha,d)\approx{\frac{({\lambda_{\max}})^{2}}{\lambda_{\max}^{2}}}=1 for large dd. Hence 1dν(α,d)→0{\tfrac{1}{d}}\nu(\alpha,d)\rto 0. ■\myqed

We now address the rate of convergence of 1d​ν​(α,d){\tfrac{1}{d}}\nu(\alpha,d) to ν∞​(α)\nu_{\infty}(\alpha), for α≥1\alpha\geq 1. The CDF corresponding to (31) is:

F⁡(x)=ℙ(λ≤x)=∫1xαtα+1​dt=1−x−αF(x)=\PP(\lambda\leq x)=\int_{1}^{x}{\frac{\alpha}{t^{\alpha+1}}}\,dt=1-x^{-\alpha} (34)

Hence F−1(y)=(1−y)−1/αF^{-1}(y)=(1-y)^{-1/\alpha}, for 0≤y≤10\leq y\leq 1, and

λk=F−1(k+1d+2)=(d+1−kd+2)−1/α\lambda_{k}=F^{-1}\left({\frac{k+1}{d+2}}\right)={\left({\frac{d+1-k}{d+2}}\right)}^{-1/\alpha}

Using (32),

∑k=1dλk≈ds​∫1d1xs​𝑑x,∑k=1dλk2≈d2​s​∫1d1x2​s​𝑑x\sum_{k=1}^{d}\lambda_{k}\approx d^{s}\int_{1}^{d}{\frac{1}{x^{s}}}\,dx,\quad\quad\sum_{k=1}^{d}\lambda_{k}^{2}\approx d^{2s}\int_{1}^{d}{\frac{1}{x^{2s}}}\,dx (35)

4 Application to Neural Networks

We now study the behaviour of the Patnaik-Pearson dimension of a data manifold under the transformations commonly seen in neural networks. We start by establishing the correspondence between the behaviour of the Patnaik-Pearson dimension for Pareto distributions described in Section 3.6, and the HTSR and SETOL theory outlined in Section 2.2. In particular, once we take account of the different notational convention (6), the critical values for the two theories are exactly in correspondence with one another.

We then investigate the behaviour of the Patnaik-Pearson dimension under various transformations of the data manifold XX - matrix multiplication by a weight matrix WW; application of softmax; application of activation functions such as ReLU; addition (as seen in skip or residual connections) interpolation and concatenation of two data manifolds; normalisation; and application of the attention kernel.

4.1 The correspondence between HTSR and SETOL and the Patnaik-Pearson dimension

Suppose we have an d×dd\times d weight matrix WW with SVD W=U​S​VTW=USV^{T}, using (1), where UU and VV are d×dd\times d orthogonal matrices, and SS is a diagonal matrix with non-negative values λ1≤λ2≤…≤λd\lambda_{1}\leq\lambda_{2}\leq\ldots\leq\lambda_{d}. Further suppose the λi\lambda_{i} have been drawn from a Pareto distribution with tail exponent α⁡(W)\alpha(W), i.e.

ℙ(λ≥t)=t−α⁡(W)\PP(\lambda\geq t)=t^{-\alpha(W)} (43)

Suppose that 𝐰¯:=1d​∑i=1d𝐰i=𝟎{\overline{\bf{w}}}:={\tfrac{1}{d}}\sum_{i=1}^{d}{\bf w}_{i}={\bf 0}, where the 𝐰i{\bf w}_{i} are the rows of WW. In this case PP(W)\PatnaikPearson(W) (considered as a data manifold of dd points in ℝd\RR^{d}) is given by ν⁡(𝝀)\nu(\blambda). Then

Y=WT​W=(U​S​VT)T​(U​S​VT)=V​ST​S​VT=V​Λ​VTY=W^{T}W=(USV^{T})^{T}(USV^{T})=VS^{T}SV^{T}=V\Lambda V^{T}

where Λ\Lambda is a diagonal matrix with entries λi2\lambda_{i}^{2}. Now, using (43),

ℙ(λ2≥t)=ℙ(λ≥t)=t−α(W)/2\PP(\lambda^{2}\geq t)=\PP(\lambda\geq\sqrt{t})=t^{-\alpha(W)/2}

In the HTSR notation, using (5), ℙ(λ2≥t)∼t1−αHTSR​(W)\PP(\lambda^{2}\geq t)\sim t^{1-\alpha_{\HTSR}(W)}. So αHTSR​(W)\alpha_{\HTSR}(W), the tail exponent of the ESD of WT​WW^{T}W, satisfies

1−αHTSR(W)=−α(W)/2⟹α(W)=2(αHTSR(W)−1)1-\alpha_{\HTSR}(W)=-\alpha(W)/2\quad\implies\quad\alpha(W)=2(\alpha_{\HTSR}(W)-1) (44)

In particular,

2≤αHTSR​(W)≤6⟹2≤α⁡(W)≤102\leq\alpha_{\HTSR}(W)\leq 6\quad\implies\quad 2\leq\alpha(W)\leq 10

and the critical value αHTSR​(W)=2\alpha_{\HTSR}(W)=2 discovered in the HTSR work corresponds to α⁡(W)=2\alpha(W)=2, which is a critical value for (33).

By consulting Figure 5, we see that for d≈1000d\approx 1000, α=2\alpha=2 corresponds to 1dPP(X)≈0.6{\tfrac{1}{d}}\PatnaikPearson(X)\approx 0.6, which is useful to keep in mind for the numerical results in the sequel.

4.2 Transformer Architecture

A generic transformer can be visualised as a stack of encoder and/or decoder layers. Each layer can be broken down into simpler components which we analyse individually. Following [25], a single encoder layer with normalisation can be realised as:

Z⁡(1)=X+MultiHead(LayerNorm(X)),Z⁡(2)=Z⁡(1)+FFN(LayerNorm(Z⁡(1)))Z(1)=X+\MultiHead(\LayerNorm(X)),\quad Z(2)=Z(1)+\FFN(\LayerNorm(Z(1))) (45)

Here XX, Z⁡(1)Z(1) and Z⁡(2)Z(2) are all N×dN\times d. A decoder layer can be realised similarly. For the purposes of this analysis, we ignore positional encodings. We define the operations appearing in (45) in more detail as follows.

Multi-head attention: For hh attention heads, define

MultiHead(X)=Concat(head1,…,headh)WO\MultiHead(X)=\Concat({\head}_{1},\ldots,{\head}_{h})W^{O} (46)

with each individual attention head defined by

headi=Attention(Qi,Ki,Vi)=softmax(XWiQ​(XWiK)Td)XWiV{\head}_{i}=\Attention(Q_{i},K_{i},V_{i})=\softmax\left({\frac{XW^{Q}_{i}{(XW^{K}_{i})}^{T}}{\sqrt{d}}}\right)XW^{V}_{i} (47)

for weight matrices WiQW^{Q}_{i}, WiKW^{K}_{i}, WiVW^{V}_{i}, WOW^{O}.

Feedforward network: The feedforward network is of the form

FFN(X)=(σ⁡(XW1+𝐛1))​W2+𝐛2\FFN(X)=(\sigma(X{W_{1}}+{\bb}_{1}))W_{2}+{\bb}_{2} (48)

for XX of shape N×dN\times d, WiW_{i} of shape d×dd\times d, and 𝐛i∈ℝd\bb_{i}\in\RR^{d}. Here σ\sigma is an activation function such as ReLU.

Layer Normalisation: Demeans and normalises each row. For a row vector 𝐱i∈ℝd\bfxi\in\RR^{d}, with mean μ\mu and standard deviation σ\sigma, then layer normalisation transforms 𝐱i↦(𝐱i−μ)/σ\bfxi\mapsto(\bfxi-\mu)/\sigma.

Therefore we need to analyse the effect on the Patnaik-Pearson dimension of a data manifold XX of each of the following operations:

  • •

    Matrix products, X↦X​WX\mapsto XW, for weight matrices WW.

  • •

    Addition of matrices, X1+X2X_{1}+X_{2}.

  • •

    Concatenation of matrices, X1⊕X2X_{1}\oplus X_{2}.

  • •

    Softmax, X↦softmax(1d​X)X\mapsto\softmax({\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{d}}}X).

  • •

    Scaled dot-product attention, Attention(Q,K,V)\Attention(Q,K,V).

  • •

    Activation functions.

  • •

    Layer normalisation.

We will see that some of these operations generally reduce Patnaik-Pearson dimension, whilst others increase it.

4.3 The Product Hypothesis

We investigate the relation between PP(XW)\PatnaikPearson(XW), PP(X)\PatnaikPearson(X) and PP(W)\PatnaikPearson(W), where XX is an N×dN\times d data manifold and WW a d×dd\times d weight matrix. We need the notion of two matrices being “in general position”.

Definition 4.1

Vector subspaces V1V_{1} and V2V_{2} of ℝd\RR^{d}, of dimensions n1n_{1}, n2n_{2} respectively, are in general position if their intersection has the smallest possible dimension,

dim(V1∩V2)=max⁡(0,n1+n2−d)\dim(V_{1}\cap V_{2})=\max(0,n_{1}+n_{2}-d)

If n1+n2≤dn_{1}+n_{2}\leq d, then V1V_{1} and V2V_{2} do not intersect, except at the origin. We say that matrices AA and BB are in general position if their eigenspaces are in general position - no eigenspace of AA overlaps with an eigenspace of BB more than dimension-counting requires.

In the following we assume that XX and WW are in general position.

Theorem 4.1

For AA and BB matrices in general position, of dimension N×dN\times d and d×md\times m respectively, with NN, dd, mm all sufficiently large, then PP(AB)≤PP(B)\PatnaikPearson(AB)\leq\PatnaikPearson(B).

Proof: Suppose the SVDs of AA and BB are

A=UA​SA​VAT,B=UB​SB​VBTA=U_{A}S_{A}V_{A}^{T},\quad B=U_{B}S_{B}V_{B}^{T}

where UAU_{A} is N×NN\times N orthogonal, SAS_{A} is N×dN\times d diagonal, with diagonal entries λi\lambda_{i} and VAV_{A} is d×dd\times d orthogonal. And similarly UBU_{B} is d×dd\times d orthogonal, SBS_{B} is d×md\times m diagonal, with diagonal entries ϕi\phi_{i} and VBV_{B} is m×mm\times m orthogonal. Then

A​B=UA​SA​(VAT​UB)​SB​VBTAB=U_{A}S_{A}(V_{A}^{T}U_{B})S_{B}V_{B}^{T}

Defining Q=VAT​UBQ=V_{A}^{T}U_{B}, and using (21), we have PP(AB)=PP(SA​QSB)\PatnaikPearson(AB)=\PatnaikPearson(S_{A}QS_{B}) and Qi​j=1d​Zi​jQ_{ij}={\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{d}}}Z_{ij}, for some Zi​j∼N⁡(0,1)Z_{ij}\sim N(0,1). Hence

(SA​Q​SB)i​j=1d​λi​Zi​j​ϕj(S_{A}QS_{B})_{ij}={\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{d}}}\lambda_{i}Z_{ij}\phi_{j}
⟹[(SA​Q​SB)T​(SA​Q​SB)]i​j=1d​(∑k=1Nλk2​Zk​i​Zk​j)​ϕi​ϕj\implies\quad[(S_{A}QS_{B})^{T}(S_{A}QS_{B})]_{ij}={\tfrac{1}{d}}(\sum_{k=1}^{N}\lambda_{k}^{2}Z_{ki}Z_{kj})\phi_{i}\phi_{j}
⟹𝔼([(SA​QSB)T​(SA​QSB)]ij)=1d​(∑k=1Nλk2)​ϕi​ϕj​δij\implies\quad\EE([(S_{A}QS_{B})^{T}(S_{A}QS_{B})]_{ij})={\tfrac{1}{d}}(\sum_{k=1}^{N}\lambda_{k}^{2})\phi_{i}\phi_{j}\delta_{ij}

So the singular values of SA​Q​SBS_{A}QS_{B} are given by αi=1d​(∑k=1Nλk2)1/2​ϕi\alpha_{i}={\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{d}}}(\sum_{k=1}^{N}\lambda_{k}^{2})^{1/2}\phi_{i}. As a result, PP(AB)=PP(SA​QSB)≤ν⁡(𝜶)=ν⁡(ϕ)=PP(B)\PatnaikPearson(AB)=\PatnaikPearson(S_{A}QS_{B})\leq\nu(\balpha)=\nu(\bphi)=\PatnaikPearson(B). ■\myqed

Corollary 4.1

For AA, BB as above, then

PP(AB)≤min⁡{PP(A),PP(B)}\PatnaikPearson(AB)\leq\min\{\PatnaikPearson(A),\PatnaikPearson(B)\} (49)

Proof: We have PP(AB)≤PP(B)\PatnaikPearson(AB)\leq\PatnaikPearson(B). Then, using (22),

PP(AB)=PP((AB)T)=PP(BT​AT)≤PP(AT)=PP(A)\PatnaikPearson(AB)=\PatnaikPearson((AB)^{T})=\PatnaikPearson(B^{T}A^{T})\leq\PatnaikPearson(A^{T})=\PatnaikPearson(A)

Hence PP(AB)≤PP(A)\PatnaikPearson(AB)\leq\PatnaikPearson(A) also, so the result follows. ■\myqed

Conjecture 4.1

For AA, BB as above, in general position, and with NN, dd, mm sufficiently large, then

1dPP(A)∗1mPP(B)≤1mPP(AB)≤min{1dPP(A),1mPP(B)}{\tfrac{1}{d}}\PatnaikPearson(A)*{\tfrac{1}{m}}\PatnaikPearson(B)\leq{\tfrac{1}{m}}\PatnaikPearson(AB)\leq\min\{{\tfrac{1}{d}}\PatnaikPearson(A),{\tfrac{1}{m}}\PatnaikPearson(B)\} (50)

This conjecture is motivated and supported by the numerical experiments shown in Figure 8, where the upper and lower bounds are defined by (49) and (50) respectively. The conjecture relies on AA and BB being in general position relative to one another, so in particular it needs to be modified for the product XT​XX^{T}X, as shown in Figure 9. In this case we have:

Lemma 4.1

Suppose that XX is N×dN\times d, with PP(X)=ν⁡(𝛌)\PatnaikPearson(X)=\nu(\blambda), for 𝛌∈ℝd\blambda\in\RR^{d} arising from the SVD decomposition of XX. Then PP(XT​X)=ν2​(𝛌)=ν⁡(𝛌2)\PatnaikPearson(X^{T}X)=\nu_{2}(\blambda)=\nu(\blambda^{2}).

Proof: Following (19) and assuming that X=XresidX=\Xresid, we start with X=U​S​VTX=USV^{T}, where SS is N×dN\times d, with diagonal elements λi\lambda_{i}, 1≤i≤d1\leq i\leq d, and 𝝀=(λi)∈ℝd\blambda=(\lambda_{i})\in\RR^{d}, then

XT​X=(U​S​VT)T​(U​S​VT)=V⁡(ST​S)​VTX^{T}X=(USV^{T})^{T}(USV^{T})=V(S^{T}S)V^{T}

and ST​SS^{T}S is d×dd\times d with diagonal elements λi2\lambda_{i}^{2}. The result follows. ■\myqed

4.4 Softmax

In general there is no clear relation between PP(softmax(X))\PatnaikPearson(\softmax(X)) and PP(X)\PatnaikPearson(X), because we have defined PP(X)\PatnaikPearson(X) to be invariant under rotations, translations and positive scalings, whereas softmax(X)\softmax(X) has no such invariance. However in “typical” cases we present a close approximation.

Definition 4.2

For an N×dN\times d data manifold XX, define softmax(X)\softmax(X) to be the row-wise softmax with inverse temperature β>0\beta>0, namely

softmax(X)i​j=exp⁡(β​Xi​j)/∑k=1dexp⁡(β​Xi​k){\softmax(X)}_{ij}=\exp(\beta X_{ij})/\sum_{k=1}^{d}\exp(\beta X_{ik}) (51)

In the limit as β→0+\beta\rto 0^{+}, then all entries tend to 1d{\tfrac{1}{d}}. So for small β\beta, softmax(X)=1d​𝟏N×d+Δ\softmax(X)={\tfrac{1}{d}}{\bf 1}_{N\times d}+\Delta, where Δ\Delta is “random noise” of shape N×dN\times d with individual terms tending to zero. However, by the definition of Patnaik-Pearson dimension, the row-wise demeaning procedure removes the 𝟏N×d{\bf 1}_{N\times d} term and PP(softmax(X))=PP(Δ)\PatnaikPearson(\softmax(X))=\PatnaikPearson(\Delta), which can take arbitrary values in the range [1,d][1,d].

In the limit as β→∞\beta\rto\infty, then softmax(X)\softmax(X) converges to a matrix with exactly one non-zero entry (of 1) in each row, in position (for row ii) given by argmaxk{Xik}\argmax_{k}\{X_{ik}\}.

For the case β=1d\beta={\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{d}}}, and N,d=O⁡(1000)N,d=O(1000), then PP(softmax(X))\PatnaikPearson(\softmax(X)) is well-approximated by

PP(softmax(X))≈PP(X)+sf(1dPP(X))\PatnaikPearson(\softmax(X))\approx\PatnaikPearson(X)+\sff({\tfrac{1}{d}}\PatnaikPearson(X)) (52)

where

sf(x)=22.0∗(x−0.001)∗exp⁡(−250​x)\sff(x)=22.0*(x-0.001)*\exp(-250x) (53)

See Figure 9. For small values of PP(X)\PatnaikPearson(X), softmax increases Patnaik-Pearson dimension, whereas for larger values of PP(X)\PatnaikPearson(X), we see that PP(softmax(X))≈PP(X)\PatnaikPearson(\softmax(X))\approx\PatnaikPearson(X).

4.5 Attention

Following the notation of [25], we define scaled dot product attention as follows. For XX of shape N×dN\times d, and weight matrices WQW^{Q}, WKW^{K},WVW^{V} all of shape d×dd\times d, define the query, key and value matrices

Q=X​WQ,K=X​WK,V=X​WVQ=XW^{Q},\quad K=XW^{K},\quad V=XW^{V} (54)

all of which are N×dN\times d. Then

Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QKTd)V\Attention(Q,K,V)=\softmax\left({\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d}}}\right)V (55)

where softmax is applied row-wise, as in (51) (with β=1\beta=1 here).

For our analysis of the Patnaik-Pearson dimension, we build up to this step by step. Given XX, WW of shape N×dN\times d and d×dd\times d respectively, the Patnaik-Pearson dimension for X​W​XTXWX^{T} is well-approximated using the formulae (50).

1NPP(XWXT)≈1dPP(X)∗1dPP(W)∗1NPP(XT){\tfrac{1}{N}}\PatnaikPearson(XWX^{T})\approx{\tfrac{1}{d}}\PatnaikPearson(X)*{\tfrac{1}{d}}\PatnaikPearson(W)*{\tfrac{1}{N}}\PatnaikPearson(X^{T})

See Figure 10.

Numerical experiments choosing NN and dd randomly between 500 and 1000, with N>dN>d, randomly choosing the Patnaik-Pearson dimension (between 1 and dd) for XX, WQW^{Q}, WKW^{K} and WVW^{V}, and calculating Attention(Q,K,V)\Attention(Q,K,V) show reasonable agreement between PP(Attention(Q,K,V))\PatnaikPearson(\Attention(Q,K,V)) and the estimate given by combining (50, 52, 53) - see Figure 10.

4.6 Activation functions : ReLU

We investigate the effect of the ReLU activation function. For XX an N×dN\times d data manifold, define

(ReLU(X))ij={Xij:Xij≥00:Xij<0,(\ReLU(X))_{ij}=\left\{\begin{aligned} X_{ij}\,:\,X_{ij}\geq 0\\ 0\,:\,X_{ij}<0\end{aligned}\right., (56)

Figure 11 shows the effect of ReLU on Patnaik-Pearson dimension. A good approximation, at least for N,d=O⁡(1000)N,d=O(1000), is

1dPP(ReLU(X))=a∗(1dPP(X))b{\tfrac{1}{d}}\PatnaikPearson(\ReLU(X))=a*({\tfrac{1}{d}}\PatnaikPearson(X))^{b} (57)

with a=exp⁡(−0.05)=0.891a=\exp(-0.05)=0.891, and b=0.69b=0.69.

4.7 Addition, Interpolation and Concatenation

For X1X_{1} and X2X_{2} both N×dN\times d, define X1+X2X_{1}+X_{2} as the usual matrix addition. As shown in Figure 12, PP(X1+X2)\PatnaikPearson(X_{1}+X_{2}) skews heavily towards min⁡{PP(X1),PP(X2)}\min\{\PatnaikPearson(X_{1}),\PatnaikPearson(X_{2})\}. As expected by Theorem 2.1, the heavier-tailed (smaller Patnaik-Pearson dimension) distribution dominates the lighter-tailed distribution.

For X0X_{0} and X1X_{1} both N×dN\times d, and 0≤t≤10\leq t\leq 1, define XtX_{t} by

(Xt)i​j=(1−t)∗(X0)i​j+t∗(X1)i​j(X_{t})_{ij}=(1-t)*(X_{0})_{ij}+t*(X_{1})_{ij} (58)

As illustrated by the example in Figure 13, if PP(X0)≤PP(X1)\PatnaikPearson(X_{0})\leq\PatnaikPearson(X_{1}), then PP(Xt)\PatnaikPearson(X_{t}) remains close to PP(X0)\PatnaikPearson(X_{0}) until tt is close to 1, before a final rapid transition towards PP(X1)\PatnaikPearson(X_{1}). This is as expected by by Theorem 2.1, in that the heavier-tailed distribution dominates the lighter-tailed distribution.

Given X1X_{1} and X2X_{2} of dimensions N1×dN_{1}\times d and N2×dN_{2}\times d respectively, define the concatenation X1⊕X2X_{1}\oplus X_{2} to be the (N1+N2)×d(N_{1}+N_{2})\times d matrix with entries

(X1⊕X2)i​j={(X1)i​j:i≤N1(X2)(i−N1)​j:N1<i≤N1+N2(X_{1}\oplus X_{2})_{ij}=\left\{\begin{aligned} (X_{1})_{ij}\,:\,i\leq N_{1}\\ (X_{2})_{(i-N_{1})j}\,:\,N_{1}<i\leq N_{1}+N_{2}\end{aligned}\right. (59)

It is apparent from Figure 14 that

PP(X1⊕X2)≈min⁡{PP(X1),PP(X2)}\PatnaikPearson(X_{1}\oplus X_{2})\approx\min\{\PatnaikPearson(X_{1}),\PatnaikPearson(X_{2})\} (60)

Again, the heavier-tailed distribution dominates.

4.8 Normalisation

For XX of shape N×dN\times d, we first demean the NN row-vectors to all have row-sum 0, then normalise so that they all have norm 1. As shown in Figure 15, for N,d=O⁡(1000)N,d=O(1000), normalisation slightly increases Patnaik-Pearson dimension, with the effect being most pronounced for small dimension.

5 Application: BERT and DeepSeek

5.1 BERT embeddings

The BERT model [6], released in 2018, was the first open-weighted state of the art LLM. We work with the BERT base model, which, at 110 million parameters, can no longer really be considered a “large” Language Model. BERT is an encoder-only model, consisting of 12 layers, with a hidden size of 768 and context length of 512 tokens. The token vocabulary is 30,522, of which 29,528 tokens are valid, and 994 invalid. Specifically, out of the first 999 tokens, five are special tokens - [PAD], [UNK], [CLS], [SEP] and [MASK] - which we keep, and the remaining 994 are [unusedN], which we seperate out as invalid. The remaining 29,523 tokens are considered to be valid.

We present results of three numerical experiments:

  1. 1.

    Common components of token embeddings. First, for the 994 invalid embeddings, the norms average 1.161, with standard deviation 0.001. Averaging the embeddings gives a common component of norm 1.154, and residualising this out reduces the average norm of the residualised embeddings to 0.125, with standard deviation 0.003. This residualisation has very little effect on the Patnaik-Pearson dimension, both pre- and post-residualisation this is 561.

    For the 29,528 valid embeddings, the norms average 1.410, with standard deviation 0.191. The average component has norm 0.937, and after residualisation the average norm is 1.176, with standard deviation 0.192.

  2. 2.

    Patnaik-Pearson dimension of the collection of valid token embeddings. We calculate the Patnaik-Pearson dimension of various collections XX of token embeddings, realised as an N×dN\times d matrix. Here d=768d=768, but it is debatable what the most natural value of NN should be. The full data manifold of all 29,528 valid token embeddings is computationally inaccessible. Furthermore, the context length of the BERT-base model is 512, which suggests N=512N=512 is a natural value to consider, although this necessarily bounds PP(X)≤512\PatnaikPearson(X)\leq 512 for any such XX. The approach we take here is to sample NN tokens without replacement from the full vocabulary of valid tokens, for NN taking various values between 100 and 10,000. Over this range, the mean (taken over multiple samples) of 1dPP(X){\tfrac{1}{d}}\PatnaikPearson(X) increases from 0.11 to 0.85. See Figure 16.

    An alternative approach, which we have not pursued, but might be considered to be semantically more meaningful, would be to select samples of genuine text from different sources, tokenize these, and calculate the Patnaik-Pearson dimension of the resulting data manifolds.

  3. 3.

    Layerwise evolution of the Patnaik-Pearson dimension. We repeatedly sample (without replacement) 512 embeddings from the full set of token embeddings. We calculate the Patnaik-Pearson dimension of the resulting data manifold as it passes through the layers of the model. As shown in Figure 17, dimension decreases steadily from an initial value of approximately 380 to approximately 120 at the final layer.

5.2 DeepSeek embeddings

We perform the same experiments for a small version of the DeepSeek-R1 model [5], namely DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B. This is a 1.5B parameter generative (decoder-only) model. It has 28 layers, compared to BERT’s 12, the hidden size is 1536, not 768, and the context length is roughly 130k, compared to 512 for BERT. The token vocabulary size is 151,643 tokens. We perform two different analyses on this model.

  1. 1.

    Patnaik-Pearson dimension of the collection of token embeddings. Since the context length is comparable to the size of the vocabulary, and dealing with a data manifold of dimension 151,643 ×\times 1536 is computationally inaccessible to us, we repeatedly sample (without replacement) from the full set of embeddings, and calculate the Patnaik-Pearson dimension of this collection. Figure 18 shows the results of sampling collections of NN tokens (for NN ranging between 500 and 20,000) and calculating the average Patnaik-Pearson dimension across all sampled collections of size NN. We can see that the average value of νd=1dPP(X){\tfrac{\nu}{d}}={\tfrac{1}{d}}\PatnaikPearson(X) increases from roughly 0.5 for N=1536N=1536 to more than 0.9 for N=20,000N=20,000. We conjecture that as NN approaches the total vocabulary size, PP(X)\PatnaikPearson(X) approaches 1536, i.e. the token embeddings exploit the full dimensionality of the embedding space.

  2. 2.

    Layerwise evolution of the Patnaik-Pearson dimension. We generate random samples of token embeddings (chosen without replacement), and the evolution of their Patnaik-Pearson dimension as they pass through the layers of the model. For the results shown in Figure 19 we generated 20 random samples of 2000 token embeddings each (so N=2000N=2000, d=1536d=1536). As shown, the initial Patnaik-Pearson dimension is on average around 1200, but is compressed dramatically to around 200 in the early layers of the model, and then remains consistently at that level until about layer 20, after which point it grows again to around 500.

6 Conclusion

In this work we have defined a novel measure of intrinsic dimension of a data manifold, which we call the Patnaik-Pearson dimension, due to its connection to Patnaik and Pearson’s moment-matching formulae. This was motivated by the application of the TwoNN intrinsic dimension estimator to a simple generative model of a data manifold. We investigate the properties of the Patnaik-Pearson dimension, and show that it has a close relation to the phenomena observed by Martin, Mahoney and Hinrichs for heavy-tailed weight matrices in neural networks, which motivated the development of their HTSR and SETOL theories. In particular, the critical values for the tail exponent for both the Patnaik-Pearson dimension and HTSR and SETOL coincide. Using a combination of theoretical and numerical techniques, we study the behaviour of the Patnaik-Pearson dimension of a data manifold under the transformations typical to neural networks - multiplication by weight matrices; application of activation functions and softmax; addition, interpolation and concatenation; layer normalisation; attention. Some of these operations typically decrease Patnaik-Pearson dimension, others tend to increase it. It remains an open question as to in what generality these results hold. We apply this theory to two examples - the BERT-base and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1 models - and observe a pattern of Patnaik-Pearson dimension decreasing as the data manifold passes through the model layers.
